Baltica This study presents new paleomagnetic data obtained for mafic dykes on Bornholm (Denmark, southwest Nuna Baltica). We provide a new 1.326 ± 0.010 Ga Bornholm Group I paleomagnetic key pole (Plat: 06◦N, Plon: P P r r e o c te a r m oz b o ri i a c n 165◦E, K: 21, A95: 6◦) for Baltica. This pole supports the low-latitude equatorial core of Nuna at 1.33 Ga, where Kola Peninsula and Northern Norway of Baltica were facing northeastern Greenland of Laurentia. ole (Plat: 06◦N, Plon: P P r r e o c te a r m oz b o ri i a c n 165◦E, K: 21, A95: 6◦) for Baltica. This pole supports the low-latitude equatorial core of Nuna at 1.33 Ga, where Kola Peninsula and Northern Norway of Baltica were facing northeastern Greenland of Laurentia. Based on statistically different magnetization directions with Group I and differences in Nb-Zr-Y systematics, we propose a separate Bornholm Group II paleomagnetic pole. This undated, poor-quality pole indicates a paleolatitude of ca. 50◦, possibly reflecting an age difference compared to Group I, accompanied with the continental drift. On Bornholm, the wide Listed and Kås dykes of uncertain age yield significantly different paleomagnetic results compared to the other studied dykes there. In addition, the virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) of these dykes are 45◦apart from each other. On the basis of similar Nb-Zr-Y systematics with the dykes of the 0.98–0.94 Ga Blekinge Dalarna Dolerite Group (Sweden) and overlapping paleomagnetic data with the high-quality 0.95–0.94 Ga paleomagnetic poles of Baltica, an early Neoproterozoic age for the magnetization is proposed. rientation was performed using a magnetic compass, and IGRF declination at each site was evaluated to correct for geographic North. The compass was always kept at least 15cm away from the rock in order to avoid possible biases of the reading. All magnetic measurements were carried out at the laboratory for solid Earth geophysics of the University of Helsinki, Finland. The magnetization of the diabases was determined using a superconducting DC- SQUID (2G) magnetometer, and an AGICO JR6-A spinner magnetometer. In general alternating field (AF) demagnetization up to 160 mT was employed to perform the directional analysis. In some cases, thermal demagnetization up to 680°C was also used. Principal component analysis to define the characteri stic remanent magnetization component (ChRM) was performed using the PmagPY software of Tauxe et al. (2010). Paleointensity measurements were perf ormed using a Shonstedt TD1 oven and a laboratory field (B lab) of 50 µT. The Coe method ( Coe, 1967), with additional pTRM and pTRM tail checks ( Riisager and Riisager , 2001) was selected for the intensity experiments. Methodology Field campaigns were conducted during 2004 and 2005. In the field, three to fifteen oriented hand samples pe r site were collected from 33 sites. The orientation was performed using a magnetic compass, and IGRF declination at each site was evaluated to correct for geographic North. The compass was always kept at least 15cm away from the rock in order to avoid possible biases of the reading. All magnetic measurements were carried out at the laboratory for solid Earth geophysics of the University of Helsinki, Finland. The magnetization of the diabases was determined using a superconducting DC- SQUID (2G) magnetometer, and an AGICO JR6-A spinner magnetometer. ABSTRACT: New paleomagnetic and rock magnetic data are presented from Paleoproterozoic 1.8 Ga shoshonitic intrusions and associated NW -SE trending lamprophyre dykes, and from undated NE-SW trending dolerite dykes at Lake Ladoga area in NW Russia. The shoshonitic intrusions and lamprophyre dykes are suggested to carry a primary 1.8 Ga remanent magnetization residing in titanomagnetite. In addition, they carry a partial remagnetiza tion component that probably resides in titanomaghemite. The dolerite dykes show a single remanence component that is thought to be a primary thermoremanent magnetization. The paleomagnetic pole positions obtained from this component are Mesoproterozoic in age (ca. 1.54 Ga). This age corresponds to that of the Salmi rapakivi massif that is found near the study area. Thus, we interpret this magnetic component to be associated with widespread thermal and magmatic events associated with rapakivi magmatism and emplacement of associated dolerite dykes. The shoshonitic intrusions represent magmas derived from enriched litospheric mantle, emplaced at upper crustal levels (Eklund et al. 1998, Konopelko & Eklund 2003). The intrusions form a conspicuous belt extending from Lake Ladoga area in NW Russia to Åland archipelago in SW Finland (Eklund et al. 1998). Paleomagnetic studies have now been carried out on three dated shoshonitic intrusions at Lake Ladoga area (Fig. 1); the Vuoksa (1802±17 Ma, U -Pb, zircon, Konopelko & Ivanikov 1996), Ojajärvi (1800 -1805 Ma, K -Ar, amphibole, Ivanikov et al. 1996) and Elisenvaara (1800±6 Ma, U -Pb, zircon, Konopelko & Vaasjoki 2002, pers. comm.) intrusions. Paleomagnetic results from the intrusions are reported in more detail in Mertanen et al. (2005) and the main conclusions are briefly described in this paper. Unfortunately, the host rocks are very weakly magnetized and do not yield stable paleomagnetic results. 3 METHODS Density and magnetic susceptibility were measured for all specimens before palaeomagnetic measurements. Remanence measurements were made using a 2G -Enterprises SQUID magnetometer and a Schoenstedt magnetometer. Demagnetizations were done both by alternating field (AF) up to peak field of 160 mT and thermally up to peak temperature of 680ºC. Mineralogical alterations were observed by monitoring the magnetic susceptibility after each thermal step. Remanence components were visually inspected by Zijderveld diagrams (Leino 1991, Zijderveld 1967) and the components were identified using principal component analysis (Kirshcvink 1980). Magnetic carriers were identified by thermomagnetic analysis by using an Agico CS2 -KLY2 Kappabridge, applying stepwise heating up to 700ºC. In order to further characterize the magnetic mineralogy, Lowrie -Fuller tests (Lowrie & Fuller 1971) were performed on selected specimens. The samples were first stepwise demagnetized in alternating fields up to 160 mT, and then given an anhysteretic remanent magnetization (ARM) in a peak AF of 200 mT and a biasing field of 0.1 mT. The ARM was then progressively AF demagnetized in peak fields up to 160 mT. The specimens were

ABSTRACT: New paleomagnetic and rock magnetic data are presented from Paleoproterozoic 1.8 Ga shoshonitic intrusions and associated NW -SE trending lamprophyre dykes, and from undated NE-SW trending dolerite dykes at Lake Ladoga area in NW Russia. The shoshonitic intrusions and lamprophyre dykes are suggested to carry a primary 1.8 Ga remanent magnetization residing in titanomagnetite. In addition, they carry a partial remagnetiza tion component that probably resides in titanomaghemite. The dolerite dykes show a single remanence component that is thought to be a primary thermoremanent magnetization. The paleomagnetic pole positions obtained from this component are Mesoproterozoic in age (ca. 1.54 Ga). This age corresponds to that of the Salmi rapakivi massif that is found near the study area. Thus, we interpret this magnetic component to be associated with widespread thermal and magmatic events associated with rapakivi magmatism and emplacement of associated dolerite dykes. Such events may also be responsible for the partial remagnetization of the shoshonites and lamprophyres. 1 INTRODUCTION The Lake Ladoga area in NW Russia forms a key location of the

Such events may also be responsible for the partial remagnetization of the shoshonites and lamprophyres. 1 INTRODUCTION The Lake Ladoga area in NW Russia forms a key location of the Fennoscandian Shield in that it preserves a record of most of the significant geological events that the shield has experienced from the Archean to the Paleozoic. The main part of the studied area was formed during the Paleoproterozoic Svecofennian orogeny at ca. 1.9-1.8 Ga. Later on the Svecofennian rocks were intruded by Mesoproterozoic ca. 1.65 -1.53 Ga rapakivi granites and associated dykes and volcanic rocks. In this study, we present paleomagnetic results from 1.8 Ga post -collisional shoshonitic intrusions (Eklund et al. 1998) and coeval lamprophyre dykes and from dolerite dykes that are thought to be related to the 1.54 Ga rapakivi granites. Geochemical, petrological and isotope age data obtained from the same sites as paleomagnetic data will be reported elsewhere (see Shebanov & Eklund 2005, Shebanov et al. 2006). Our palaeomagnetic results suggest two major phases of martite-microplaty hematite formation or recrystallisation, and thus iron ore magnetisation, in the Hamersley Province. The first corresponds to the steep southwest-directed regional remagnetisation, and could have occurred late during, or after, the Ophthalmia Orogeny (ca. 2400 to 2200 Ma). An alternative interpretation is that it could have formed during the 1800-1650 Ma Ashburton Orogeny. This event was important for hematite/martite ore formation in both the eastern (Mt Whaleback, Ore Bodies 23 and 25, Area C) and central (Tom Price and Paraburdoo deposits) Hamersley Province, but there is no sign of it in the western Hamersley Province (i.e., the Barrett-Lennard deposit and the M-(mpl h) ores in Channar deposit). The second phase, most likely related to the Ashburton Orogeny (ca. 1800 to 1650 Ma), is dominant in the western-central Hamersley Province (Barrett-Lennard and Channar deposits), and it strongly reworked the iron deposits in central Hamersley Province (Tom Price and Paraburdoo deposits), but had little impact on the deposits in eastern Hamersl

Province (Mt Whale back, Ore Bodies 23 and 25, and Area C deposits). We thus see a mixed, but dominantly the younger, magnetic overprint in the central Hamersley Province deposits. Palaeomagnetic results further suggest that the first phase of ore genesis (ca. 2200 Ma) occurred when the Pilbara was at a palaeolatitude of ca. 50°, whereas the second (possibly minor) phase (ca. 1700 Ma) occurred at a tropical palaeolatitude. We have also established a comprehensive petrophysical database for the Hamersley Province rock units and iron deposits during the course of this project. The ca. 755 Ma NE-trending dyke intrusions caused localised magnetite mineralisation only (i.e., the small magnetite ore bodies in contact with a NE-trending dyke in the Channar Mine). We see no evidence for any Mesozoic to Tertiary mineralisation in the in-situ deposits apart from the formation of a surface hard cap. A remanence carried by hematite, directed mostly downward towards the northwest with a moderate to shallow inclination, was found from both mines. The directions from the Mt Newman mine were much better grouped than those from the Mt Tom Price mine. On the basis of comparison with palaeomagnetic directions of known age, Porath and Chamalaun (1968) concluded that the mineralisation dated back to the Precambrian, not the Phanerozoic. Clark and Schmidt (1986) reported results from another magnetic investigation in the region. They studied both BIF and ore bodies at the Mt Tom Price and Paraburdoo mines. target_context.excerpt: Paleomagnetic Study on the Permian Rocks of the Indochina Block and Its Implications for Paleogeographic Conﬁguration and Northward Drifting of Cathaysialand in the Paleo-Tethys Yonggang Yan1 , Baochun Huang 2 , Donghai Zhang 2 , Punya Charusiri 3, and Apivut Veeravinantanakul 3 1Guangdong Provincial Key Lab of Geodynamics and Geohazards, School of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Sun Yat-

The drift of Gondwana-derived blocks across the Tethys has remained unclear speci ﬁcally because one of the largest components, Indochina, has remained unconstrained by paleomagnetism during the late Paleozoic, the interval comprising theﬁrst half of its journey towards the Eurasian landmass. Hence, we report a paleomagnetic study of Early-Middle Permian limestones from central Thailand yielding a high-quality data set for the Indochina Block with probable primary origin. The magnetization yields a paleomagnetic pole at 34.1°N, 331.7°E (K =4 5 . 4 ,A 95 = 5.7°) corresponding to a paleolatitude of 21.2 ± 5.7°S at the center of the study area (15°N, 101°E) and supporting a tropical restoration for late Paleozoic Indochina.

The Nan-Uttaradit Suture subsequently lost its status as the closed remnant of the main Paleo-Tethys Ocean and is now increasingly accepted as a back-arc basin. The boundaries between Indochina and the other blocks (e.g., Song Ma suture to South China, Bentong-Raub suture to East Malaya, Median Sumatra suture to West Sumatra) have become basically clear following the work of Ueno (2003), Sone and Metcalfe (2008), and Ueno et al. (2012), although a contrasting assessment has been given by Cai and Zhang (2009). The study area, petrographically the Khao Khwang Platform, geotectonically is the western margin of the Indochina Block. It comprises the area to the east of the Nan-Uttaradit Suture Zone, north of Mae Ping Fault, and west of the Nam Duk Basin (Figure 1; Ridd et al., 2011). The Permian succession in the Saraburi area com- prises the Saraburi Group and incorporates the Sap Bon, Khao Khad, Pang Asok, Nong Pong, Khao Khwang, and Phu Phe formations. In the Nakhon Sawan-Phetchahun area the Permian succession comprises the Tak Fa Formation (Figure 2). Is the Pyrrhotite Record Reliable? The presence of pyrrhotite (Fe7S8) is increasingly being reported from sediments, although geochemical con- ditions required for the formation of pyrrhotite are poorly understood and many factors are considered to potentially contribute to the formation of ferromagnetic iron sul ﬁdes (greigite and pyrrhotite). These include the availability of ﬁne iron-containing mineral and sulfate grains, bioactivity and speci ﬁc redox conditions. Combining our results with previous data from the South Shetland Islands and the Antarctic Peninsula, we calculated the paleopoles for 110 Ma and 55 Ma for the South Shetland Islands and the Antarctic Peninsula. After assessing the results from these AF and TH pilot specimens, most of the remaining specimens were ﬁrst AF demagnetized at steps of 15 and 30 mT and then TH demagnetized at steps of 450, 500, 520, 540, 560 and 580 ◦C, plus steps of 610, 630 and 650 ◦C for about half of them. To characterize the magnetic minerals, 11 typical specimens were subjected to saturation isothermal remanent magnetization (SIRM) testing. After initial AF demagnetization at 150 mT , each specimen was magnetized in a direct ﬁeld in 14 steps up to 900 mT using a Sapphire Instruments SI-6 DC pulse magnetizer, and then it was AF step demagnetized in 11 steps to 150 mT . Also, hysteresis loop measurements were obtained using a Lake Shore Cryotonics PMC Micromag vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM) model 3900–04 on two chip samples from each of sites 5, 8, 18 and 19. Our results favor a rock-magnetic origin for the observed shallow inclinations from the Qaidam Basin. Interpreting the 26 8 shallowing of inclination for the HTC component from the XQB section by northward tectonic transport would require ;2500 km of latitudinal motion in ,10 m.y., implying a velocity .25 cm/yr. Paleo- magnetism can determine net vertical-axis rotation of crustal blocks over 10 6±109 yr (Beck et al., 1986; Chen et al., 1993a; Gilder et al., 1996). Here we report paleomagnetic data from the interior of the Qaidam Basin that limit rotation to #58 over the past 30 m.y. The Qaidam Basin (Fig. 1) is a relatively low elevation region of 1.2 3 10 5 km2 in the northeast Tibetan Plateau bounded by the Altyn Tagh fault to the northwest, the Kunlun fault to the south, and the Nan Shan fold-and-thrust belt to the northeast. Compared to complexly de- formed surrounding areas, the Qaidam Basin shows only limited de- formation of the Cretaceous to Tertiary sedimentary cover (Meyer et al., 1998). This change in elevation and intensity of deformation is attributed to higher strength of the Qaidam crust (Zhu et al., 1995) compared to surrounding regions that underwent compressional defor- mation and attendant crustal thickening. Although these characteristics make the Qaidam Basin an important target for studying vertical-axis rotations related to the Himalaya-Tibetan orogen, outcrop areas within the basin are limited and often dif®cult to access. The magmas erupted onto basement rocks: deformed Palaeozoic sediments and granitic rocks, and at some localities (e.g. Mt Bygalorie and Wilga Tank, El Capitan) upon Cenozoic sediments that unconformably overlie basement. The magmas are interpreted to have followed shallow depressions that have since eroded leaving the lava ﬂows exposed as lobate hills and ridgelines. The leucitite mineral assemblage in New South Wales (NSW) is characterized by iddingsitized olivine and less commonly by clinopyroxene phenocrysts set in a groundmass of clinopyroxene, leucite, titanomagnetite (and titanomaghemite), nepheline and mica. Sparse, microscopic pegmatoid veinlets have been commonly ob- served and are comprised of similar minerals with the exception of olivine, which is absent from these veins (Cundari 1973). All lavas along the Cosgrove track exhibit OIB-like trace element patterns (Davies et al. 2015). The leucitites are silica-undersaturated and, compared to their basaltic counterparts in Queensland, composi- tions have higher concentrations of Ti, Mg, K, P , Cr, Ni, Zn and trace elements, and lower Si, Al and Na concentrations. is study is to provide a new high-quality palaeomagnetic pole for mid- Miocene Australia using results from leucitite lavas in Eastern Australia, given their precise 40Ar/39Ar ages. We review published palaeomagnetic data for Australia during the mid- Miocene and examine palaeosecular variation during the 15–17 Ma interval. The average palaeomagnetic direction from leucitite lavas ( D = 190.2 ◦, I = 57.1◦, k = 33.9, a95 = 6.7◦) and the palaeomagnetic pole (λ =− 80.2◦, φ = 95.4◦, K = 20.5, A95 = 8.6◦, N = 15, Q = 5) are statistically indistinguishable from early mid-Miocene poles from Nandewar V olcano and from the Port Campbell and Glenample Formations, demonstrating that older palaeomagnetic results can be robust despite outdated methodology (e.g. blanket demagnetization, few sam- ples per site). We evaluate palaeosecular variation (PSV) during the mid-Miocene utilizing the combined data set ( N = 85/93; cut-off), and calculate a mid-Miocene combined pole for Australia (λ =− 80.0 ◦, φ = 103.6◦, K = 26.9, A95 = 3.0◦, N = 85, Q = 6). The pole yields a palaeolatitude estimate for the Cosgrove Hotspot of λ15 − 17Ma = 40.3◦S ± 3.0◦, consistent with the present-day inferred location of the Cosgrove Hotspot at 40.5 ◦S. Alternating field (AF) and thermal stepwise demagnetization revealed northwestern characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) directions with low positive inclinations (mean: Dm =303.2◦, Im =12.2◦, N =10, α 95 =14.5◦, K =12.0). A paleomagnetic pole was calculated for the Huanchaca sills (HU 225.7◦E, 30.1◦N, A95 =9.9◦) which is classified with reliability index R =5. section_candidates.excerpt: 0–1000 Ma) Rodinia was being formed, and the Amazonian Craton, presently in Paleomagnetism northern South America, was an important piece in this scenario. Recently a megacontinent named Umkondia Amazonian Craton composed by Amazonia/West Africa, Congo/Sa˜o Francisco, Kalahari and India was proposed to have existed at Mesoproterozoic 1100 Ma. We present a paleomagnetic study on the well-dated (U-Pb, baddeleyite) 1112 Ma mafic sills from the Umkondia Huanchaca Intrusive Suite, western Mato Grosso State (Amazonian Craton) in order to test the proposed Rodinia supercontinent configuration of Umkondia. In this study, we mainly P P a a l l e e o o m lat a i g tu n d e e ti s v m ar iations report a new paleopole (54.2 ◦S, 111.4 ◦E, A95 =5.1◦) obtained from the upper Jiayuan Formation in the middle Rodinia assembly Huaibei Group by incorporating our new data with the previously published virtual geomagnetic poles. That average pole passed a positive fold test and a positive reversal test, along with the pole’s distinctiveness from younger poles of the NCC, support the interpretation that the remanence is primary. New detrital zircon U–Pb age analyses of a sandstone sample of the Jiayuan Formation and the mafic sills intruding the overlying strata dated previously together constrain the depositional age of the Jiayuan Formation to be between ca. 1089 and ca. 945 Ma. Our new data, incorporated with other poles previously reported from the Huaibei Group and the mafic sills intruding the strata, reveal that the NCC underwent large-scale paleolatitudinal shifts from the polar region to low latitudes across the transition between Mesoproterozoic and Neoproterozoic. The Xiao Qaidam section A (XQA section) is composed of 22 sites in dark red sandstones covering ;200 m of folded strata in the Oligocene Lower Gancaigou Formation (Qinghai Bureau of Geology and Mineral Re- sources, 1991). Only seven sites provided well-determined site-mean characteristic magnetization directions (Fig. 2B) because the coarser sandstones produced erratic thermal-demagnetization behavior (Fig. DR1, A). Concentration of unblocking temperatures in the 650±685 8C range for the characteristic component (Fig. DR1, B) and rock-magnetic experiments indicate that this magnetization is carried by hematite. One site-mean direction was discarded on the basis of its aberrant direction that probably resulted from local structural complexity in this folded section. Paleo- magnetism can determine net vertical-axis rotation of crustal blocks over 10 6±109 yr (Beck et al., 1986; Chen et al., 1993a; Gilder et al., 1996). Here we report paleomagnetic data from the interior of the Qaidam Basin that limit rotation to #58 over the past 30 m.y. The Qaidam Basin (Fig. 1) is a relatively low elevation region of 1.2 3 10 5 km2 in the northeast Tibetan Plateau bounded by the Altyn Tagh fault to the northwest, the Kunlun fault to the south, and the Nan Shan fold-and-thrust belt to the northeast. Compared to complexly de- formed surrounding areas, the Qaidam Basin shows only limited de- formation of the Cretaceous to Tertiary sedimentary cover (Meyer et al., 1998). This change in elevation and intensity of deformation is attributed to higher strength of the Qaidam crust (Zhu et al., 1995) compared to surrounding regions that underwent compressional defor- mation and attendant crustal thickening. Although these characteristics make the Qaidam Basin an important target for studying vertical-axis rotations related to the Himalaya-Tibetan orogen, outcrop areas within the basin are limited and often dif®cult to access. carrier_identity_candidates.excerpt: andwiched by the Siberia Craton (SIB) and the North China Craton (NCC), plays an essential role for understanding the late stage evolution of the Paleo‐Asian Ocean and the early stage evolution of the Mongol ‐Okhotsk Ocean. Here, a paleomagnetic study is performed for the ﬁrst time on the Early Permian volcanic strata in the Bayandun region of northeastern Mongolia and the data are used to uncover the late Paleozoic paleoposition of the MOB and better understand the evolution of both oceans. Zircon U ‐Pb dating results reveal an emplacement age of 283 ± 3 Ma for the studied volcanic strata. Rock magnetic analyses identify that titanium ‐poor magnetite is the main magnetic carrier. Characteristic remanent magnetization isolated from seven sites shows consistent reverse polarity, corresponding to the Permo ‐Carboniferous (Kiaman) Reverse Superchron. Site‐mean directions pass fold tests, and an Early Permian paleomagnetic pole is calculated for the MOB at λ/φ = −14.9°N/76.8°E (A95 = 5.7°) with N = 7 sites. Comparison with published Permian paleomagnetic poles from surrounding blocks indicates that (1) the MOB should have welded with the NCC before the Early Permian or was at least very close to it. Conclusions In order to uncover the Late Paleozoic paleogeographic position of the MOB and further understand evolu- tion of both the Paleo‐Asian Ocean and the Mongol‐Okhotsk Ocean, a paleomagnetic study is performed on the Early Permian volcanic strata in the Bayandun region of northeastern Mongolia. Here, we report the first Permo-Carboniferous paleomagnetic data from the Songliao-Jiamusi block, aiming to constrain its relative paleoposition with respect to Mongolia. A stable characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) was isolated from 313–292 Ma volcanic-sedimentary sequences of the Dashizhai Formation. The ChRM yields a primary record of the geomagnetic field with positive fold, reversal and paleosecular variation tests. Along with published paleomagnetic data and geological constraints, we proposed a new reconstruction for the CAOB at 300 Ma. Our model posits that the Songliao-Jiamusi and Mongolia blocks were welded into the unified Amuria

re preserved on both sides of the NHS (Feng et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2020). A suite of Upper Carboniferous to Upper Permian volcanic-sedimentary sequences outcrop in the Ulanhot area (Figures 1b and 2; IMBGMR, 1991). section_candidates.excerpt: the existence Abstract Amuria formed in the late Paleozoic through amalgamation of the Mongolia and Songliao- Jiamusi blocks in the eastern Central Asian Orogenic Belt (CAOB). The exact timing of the assembly is critical towards unraveling the Phanerozoic evolution of the Paleo-Asian Ocean (PAO) and assembly of the Asian blocks in Pangea. Here, we report the first Permo-Carboniferous paleomagnetic data from the Songliao-Jiamusi block, aiming to constrain its relative paleoposition with respect to Mongolia. A stable characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) was isolated from 313–292 Ma volcanic-sedimentary sequences of the Dashizhai Formation. The ChRM yields a primary record of the geomagnetic field with positive fold, reversal and paleosecular variation tests. Along with published paleomagnetic data and geological constraints, we proposed a new reconstruction for the CAOB at 300 Ma. Our model posits that the Songliao-Jiamusi and Mongolia blocks were welded into the unified Amuria block situated along the northern side of the PAO (∼34°N). On the southern side of the PAO, the Xilinhot and North China blocks were situated at equatorial paleolatitudes and were not amalgamated with Amuria until 250 Ma. This finding provides new insights into Asian paleogeography and the recons

The western margin of the Songliao-Jiamusi block developed on Precambrian basement whereas the interi- or Songliao basin is floored by Mesozoic and late Paleozoic basement (Qian et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2018). Si- lurian to Carboniferous arc-related igneous rocks that recorded bilateral subduction of the Nenjiang Ocean are preserved on both sides of the NHS (Feng et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2020). A suite of Upper Carboniferous to Upper Permian volcanic-sedimentary sequences outcrop in the Ulanhot area (Figures 1b and 2; IMBGMR, 1991). From oldest to youngest, the Upper Carboniferous to Lower Permian Dashizhai Formation comprises neritic basic to felsic lavas, tuffs and interbedded sandstones with abundant branchi- opod and Crinoid fossils ( Neospirifer sp., Schizophoria sp.); the Lower-Middle Permian Zhesi Formation includes the previously defined Wujiatun Formation and consists of slates, bioclastic limestones, shales and sandstones, developing branchiopods, reefs, crinoides and bryozoans; the Upper Permian Linxi Formation comprises slates, sandstones and interbedded felsic volcaniclastic rocks with abundant bivalves and the Angara genus of phytoliths (IMBGMR, 1991). Pyrrhotite, however, is difficult to identify with the particular suite of room temperature rock magnetic analyses performed here. Other kinds of magnetizations were not investigated. The contribution by the LC1 phase to the remanence is, however, minimal. The MC1 peak around ∼130 mT in most of our samples is interpreted as high coercivity titanomagnetite (Peters & Dekkers, 2003) and the high coercivity phases with peaks above or around 1,000 mT (i.e., HC2) are provi - sionally identified hematite, as goethite typically only becomes magnetized at much higher fields in IRM (Hu et al., 2013; Rochette et al., 2005). The HC2 phase is only seen in three samples as a negligible contributor to IRM. The high coercivity peaks between 444 and 560 mT (i.e., HC1) present in many of the samples is within the range of very fine-grained detrital hematite (e.g., Swanson-Hysell et al., 2019). HC1 is present in most samples as a very minor contributor to IRM, and is not considered an important carrier of remanence, because none of the specimens carried stable magnetizations after demagnetization above 540°C. Two mudstone samples yielded higher l

coercivity peaks at ∼54 mT (i.e., LC2) in combination with medium-coercivity peaks around ∼130 mT (i.e., MC1) and small peaks at ∼269 mT (i.e., MC2). Both the LC2 and MC1 peaks are interpreted to be magnetite of varying coercivity (e.g., Peters & Dekkers, 2003), with the LC2 peak dominating the remanence. The higher coercivity peak is within the range expected for hematite (i.e., 140–800 mT; Hu et al., 2013; Slotznick et al., 2016), and is interpreted as pigmentary hematite (Swanson-Hysell et al., 2019) with a negligible contribution to the overall remanence. The dominant magnetic phase in most of the samples is thus interpreted to be magnetite of variable coerciv - ity. NRM:IRM ratios in most samples are in the 1:1,000 range and are consistent with the NRM largely being a post-depositional or depositional remanent magnetization (pDRM or DRM). Samples KWV716.74 and KWV1764.7 have an NRM:IRM ratio in the 1:100 range. Both of these samples have a main coercivity peak at ∼130 mT and are dominated by magnetite. Magnetization carried in these samples is more likely secondary magnetizations, possibly a thermal remanent magnetization (TRM) due to the heating effects of dolerite intru - sions, or a chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) due to diagenetic alteration in response to burial

However, sample KWV716.74 is not in the vicinity of an intrusion, but does share an elevated NRM intensity with samples that are associated with intrusions. KWV1764.7 is near a fairly thick dolerite intersection (no. 14) in the core and is likely baked. Only three of our test samples displayed remanence dominated by two magnetic phases. These were KWV191.13 and KWV996.51, representing mudstones, and KWV916.45, which is a fine-grained sandstone. These samples showed both LC1 or LC2 peaks (i.e., low coercivity magnetite/pyrrhotite?) as one dominant phase, and MC1 (high coercivity magnetite) or MC2 (hematite?) peaks as a second dominant phase in combination with smaller peaks (e.g., HC1 or HC2). For these samples, the Fuller test that shows NRM:IRM ratios between the 1:1,000 and 1:100 range cannot be interpreted easily, as the test was originally calibrated for magnetite. The pronounced concave upward shape of the NRM:IRM curves suggests that magnetically soft phases (LC1 and LC2) are not efficient carriers of weak field remanent magnetization. Introduction Within the southern main Karoo Basin, the late Carboniferous to mid-Jurassic Karoo Supergroup of South Africa (Figure 1) represents a 12-km thick, laterally continuous, clastic sedimentary succession that was deposited in a retro-arc foreland setting in response to subduction and accretionary tectonics along the southwest margin of Gondwana (Johnson et al., 1996, 2006). During the Permian, an interplay between regional tectonics, an icehouse to greenhouse climatic transition, and a marine incursion resulted in deepening of the southern main Karoo Basin and deposition of the Ecca Group (Catuneanu et al., 2002; Cole, 1992). The Ecca Group is well documented in the southwest section of the basin in terms of lithostratigraphy (Cole, 1992; Wickens, 1994), geochronology (Bangert et al., 1999; Belica, Tohver, Flint, et al., 2017; Fildani et al., 2007, 2

al., 2015, 2016; Turner, 1999) and magnetostratigraphy (Abubakre & De Kock, 2021; Belica, Tohver, Flint, et al., 2017; Lanci et al., 2013; Tohver et al., 2015). It, however, remains underexplored in the southeast where outcrops are fewer, the lithofacies very different (Johnson, 2009), and the stratigraphy is interrupted by dolerite sills of the ca. 183 Ma Karoo large igneous province (KLIP). However, the lack of coeval paleomagnetic data renders the putative connection ambiguous. Here we report new paleomagnetic results obtained from seven ca. 770 Ma mafic sills in SCC that provide new critical constraints on the issue. The data quality is assured by a positive regional tilt test, a reversal test, and by adequately averaging-out paleosecular variation. The differences between these two orientation methods are less than 3° (most <2°), suggesting no significant magnetic anomalies in the region. 3. Methods and Results All drill cores were cut into 1–2 specimens of 1–2.2 cm in length. Thermal susceptibility was measured using a KLY-4S Kappabridge with heating from −192 to 700°C and cooling back to room temperature. Representative samples were selected for isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM), backfield demagnetization of saturation IRM (SIRM), and thermal demagnetization of the three-axis IRM experiments (Lowrie, 1990) to determine the magnetic carriers. Progressive alternating field (AF) demagnetizations up to a field of 140 mT were applied on several representative samples of the Guzhang sills. Most of the samples were subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetization performed on ASC-TD-48 and MMTSC furnaces. Remanent magnetizations were measured using a 2G-755-4K cryogenic magnetometer and a JR-6A spinner magnetometer. Demagnetization steps of the samples from the sills and baked rocks ranged from 50 to 80°C in the

Demagnetization steps of the samples from the sills and baked rocks ranged from 50 to 80°C in the low temperatures, subsequently 5–20°C until 595°C. Meanwhile, the unbaked samples from red beds were demagnetized with temperature intervals of 5–100°C until 690°C. Demagnetization and remanence measurement were both completed in a magnetically shielded room in which the residual field is <300 nT. All the aforementioned experiments were conducted in the Paleomagnetism and Environmental Magnetism Laboratory (PMEML) at the China University of Geosciences, Beijing (CUGB). Based on these measurements, several samples were selected for magnetic hysteresis loop analyses using a MicroMag 3900 Vibrating Sample Magnetometer at the Institute of Geophysics, the China Earthquake Administration. However, the age of the Liantuo Formation remains highly controversial (e.g., Abstract A paleogeographic affinity of the south China craton (SCC) with India in the Neoproterozoic has long been advocated based on lines of geological evidence. However, the lack of coeval paleomagnetic data renders the putative connection ambiguous. Here we report new paleomagnetic results obtained from seven ca. 770 Ma mafic sills in SCC that provide new critical constraints on the issue. The data quality is assured by a positive regional tilt test, a reversal test, and by adequately averaging-out paleosecular variation. Our data, together with coeval poles from the global paleomagnetic database, support a reconstruction in which the SCC was connected with India at ca. 770 Ma via linkages with smaller continental blocks. The SCC-India landmass was located at high-to-mid latitudes and far from Laurentia and Australia, which were located at low latitudes at ca. 770 Ma. XIAO QAIDAM RESULTS Southwest of Xiao Qaidam, paleomagnetic samples were collected across a broad anticline in two stratigraphic sections (Fig. 2A). The Xiao Qaidam section A (XQA section) is composed of 22 sites in dark red sandstones covering ;200 m of folded strata in the Oligocene Lower Gancaigou Formation (Qinghai Bureau of Geology and Mineral Re- sources, 1991). Only seven sites provided well-determined site-mean characteristic magnetization directions (Fig. 2B) because the coarser sandstones produced erratic thermal-demagnetization behavior (Fig. DR1, A). Concentration of unblocking temperatures in the 650±685 8C range for the characteristic component (Fig. DR1, B) and rock-magnetic experiments indicate that this magnetization is carried by hematite. One site-mean direction was discarded on the basis of its aberrant direction that probably resulted from local structural complexity in this folded section. The remaining site-mean directions pass a fold test (Mc- Fadden, 1990) at 99% con®dence; the single normal-polarity site-mean direction is indistinguishable from the antipode of the mean computed from the reverse-polarity sites. Paleo- magnetism can determine net vertical-axis rotation of crustal blocks over 10 6±109 yr (Beck et al., 1986; Chen et al., 1993a; Gilder et al., 1996). Here we report paleomagnetic data from the interior of the Qaidam Basin that limit rotation to #58 over the past 30 m.y. The Qaidam Basin (Fig. 1) is a relatively low elevation region of 1.2 3 10 5 km2 in the northeast Tibetan Plateau bounded by the Altyn Tagh fault to the northwest, the Kunlun fault to the south, and the Nan Shan fold-and-thrust belt to the northeast. Compared to complexly de- formed surrounding areas, the Qaidam Basin shows only limited de- formation of the Cretaceous to Tertiary sedimentary cover (Meyer et al., 1998). This change in elevation and intensity of deformation is attributed to higher strength of the Qaidam crust (Zhu et al., 1995) compared to surrounding regions that underwent compressional defor- mation and attendant crustal thickening. We report 19 new data from only the second paleomagnetic investigation of this unit. Standard alternating 20 field and thermal demagnetization methods were used to isolate characteristic 21 magnetizations from seven outcrops at three locations within the Kashmir Valley, NW India. 22 Analysis of four sections (14 individual cooling units) from close to Srinagar, that together 23 form a tectonically coherent sequence spanning ~3 km of stratigraphy, yield a single- 24 component, primary magnetization with a mean direction of Dec: 134.8°, Inc: 55.3° (α95 = 25 8.9°, k = 21.0). An inclination-only mean of 52.5° (α95 = 8.9°, k = 47.2) gives a paleolatitude of 26 ~33°S (± 5°). A paleopole of 110.5°E 8.4°S (A95 = 10.7) is also calculated. Four block samples were collected at this 214 site (PT 4.1 - PT 4.4) across a 30-40 m of stratigraphy. 215 3.2.3 Sampling method 216 At each outcrop oriented blocks (ideally within ±2° in both the horizontal and vertical planes), 217 500–700 cm3, were collected from discrete cooling units (all bar one are flows, the other is a 218 gabbroic dyke). Each individual cooling-unit block sample, therefore, represents a 219 paleomagnetic ‘site’ because the sample should provide an instantaneous record of the 220 geomagnetic field a shortly after the magma had crystallized and the magnetic grains cooled 221 below their blocking temperatures. There is, however, potential for blocks collected in this 222 way to record small sampling-related orientation biases, which is not really a problem with 223 field-based drill-cored collections. Therefore, in an attempt to minimize this effect, we aimed 224 to select reference surfaces with very different orientations to the others in the section. 225 Magnetic bearings were corrected to ‘true’ using the International Geomagnetic Field Model, 226 version 11; at the time of sampling the offset was ∼1°W. 227 3.2.4 Laboratory methodology 228 The bulk of the samples were prepared and analyzed at the University of Hong Kong 229 Paleomagnetic Lab

features and they are not well dated. In this study we use paleomagnetic data to constrain the timing of the poorly dated Decaturville impact structure (Missouri) and the Weaubleau feature (Missouri), interpreted to be an impact structure, to evaluate the possibility of a serial impact event. A post depositional, mid Permian pole derived from impact-related breccias at Decaturville, as well as crosscutting relationships, show a Pennsylvanian-mid Permian age for the structure. A post- tilting Late Mississippian pole from deformed strata at Weaubleau indicates that the deformation event can be no younger than Late Mississippian. Our results demonstrate that the Decaturville and Weaubleau structures are of different ages

features and they are not well dated. In this study we use paleomagnetic data to constrain the timing of the poorly dated Decaturville impact structure (Missouri) and the Weaubleau feature (Missouri), interpreted to be an impact structure, to evaluate the possibility of a serial impact event. A post depositional, mid Permian pole derived from impact-related breccias at Decaturville, as well as crosscutting relationships, show a Pennsylvanian-mid Permian age for the structure. A post- tilting Late Mississippian pole from deformed strata at Weaubleau indicates that the deformation event can be no younger than Late Mississippian. GEOLOGICAL SETTING The Keurusselka¨ impact structure is situated within the Central Finland Granitoid Complex (hereafter called CFGC) (Nironen 2003). CFGC was formed 1890–1860 Ma ago during the peak phase of the Svecofennian orogeny, where the growing Svecofennian island arc system collided against the Archaean continent. Continental deformation, metamorphism and crust forming magmatism occurred at approximately 1900–1800 Ma. The granitoids with biotite, hornblende, titanite, apatite, magnetite, and zircon (Ka ¨ hko¨ nen 2005) are predominant rocks in the CFGC together with schists and gneisses. Arc-type volcanic rocks, which are metamorphosed at high-T and low-P amphibolite facies, characterize also this part of the Paleoproterozoic crust. According to Ka ¨ hko¨ nen (2005), the Svecofennian granitic bedrock resulted from remelting of older approximately 2100 Ma crust of several microcontinents. , our group made an observation of narrow monomictic breccia veins from one of the drill cores drilled close to the central uplift area (Fig. 1B). The breccia has a resemblance to the impact-related lithic parautochtonous impact breccias generally formed beneath the crater ﬂoor in relatively low pressures (French and Koeberl 2010). The angular and slightly roundish gneiss clasts are embedded in a ﬁne-grained dark gray matrix of the same material. Thin section analysis of these breccia samples showed hydrothermal alteration and chloritization in minerals (Raiskila et al. 2011). Different sulﬁdes like chalcopyrite, pyrite, and trace amounts of pyrrhotite were detected. PDFs in quartz were not found, but few small (less than 1 mm) optically isotropic areas were noticed. Microprobe studies revealed these areas as very ﬁne-grained clay minerals (chlorite, illite, smectite-group). Based on their appearance, it seems that they have originated from glass. The geochemical analysis is currently ongoing, and results will be reported in the near future. Planar Deformation Features The shock produced Planar Deformation Features (PDFs) in quartz, and feldspar is a clear evidence of a hypervelocity impact, as they are distinct from nonimpact deformation features (French and Koeberl 2010). According to thermomagnetic results (Fig. 5 and Table 2), most of the samples show two or three magnetic phases. The ﬁrst weak phase occurs around 120 –150 . The second phase, T C, with higher coercivity, occurs at approximately 330 , indicating most likely the presence of pyrrhotite. The third phase with Curie temperatures of approximately 560–580 Ca n d occurrence of Hopkinson peaks indicates almost pure magnetite of single-domain (SD) and ⁄ or pseudo-single- domain (PSD) type. Some thermomagnetic curves show also possible weak traces of hematite around 680 C. Most samples indicated irreversible behavior of heating and cooling cycle, which is typical for magnetite, and indicates instability of ferromagnetic minerals with formation of new magnetic phases (Dunlop and O¨ zdemir 1997). E-mail: selen.raiskila@helsinki.ﬁ (Received 25 March 2011; revision accepted 16 August 2011) Abstract–There are 31 proven impact structures in Fennoscandia—one of the most densely crater-populated areas of the Earth. The recently discovered Keurusselka ¨ impact structure (62 08¢ N, 24 37¢ E) is located within the Central Finland Granitoid Complex, which formed 1890–1860 Ma ago during the Svecofennian orogeny. It is a deeply eroded complex crater that yields in situ shatter cones with evidence of shock metamorphism, e.g., planar deformation features in quartz. New petrophysical and rock magnetic results of shocked and unshocked target rocks of various lithologies combined with paleomagnetic studies are presented. The suggested central uplift with shatter cones is characterized by increased magnetization and susceptibility. The presence of magnetite and pyrrhotite was observed as carriers for the remanent magnetization. Four different remanent magnetization directions were isolated: (1) a characteristic Svecofennian target rock component A with a mean direction of D = 334.8 , I = 45.6 , a 95 =1 4 . 9 yielding a pole (Plat = 51.1 , Plon = 241.9 , A95 = 15.1 ), (2) component B, D

Components C and E are considered much younger, possibly Neoproterozoic overprints, compared with the components A and B. The pole of component B corresponds with the 1120 Ma pole of Salla diabase dyke and is in agreement with the 40Ar ⁄ 39Ar age of 1140 Ma from a pseudotachylitic breccia vein in a central part of the structure. Therefore, component B could be related to the impact, and thus represent the impact age. Fennoscandia is statistically one of the most densely crater-populated parts of the Earth (Henkel and Pesonen 1992; Abels et al. 2002; Dypvik et al. 2008) as most of the craters are exposed. Altogether, 31 impact structures, with ages from approximately 2400 Ma to approximately 0.004 Ma, have been discovered

If the magnetite and hematite did indeed acquire their remanence during high ‐temperature oxidation during initial cooling of the lavas, then the directions should be similar. That they are slightly different could be the result of differences in the duration of remanence acquisition during cooling. The residual remanence intensity above 580 °C versus NRM intensity (Int 580/IntNRM) of the 182 samples containing hematite reveals two major populations of samples: one in the range of 0.2 –0.4 and the other 0.8–1.0, with an average value of 0.65 (Figure S1). Considering the saturation magnetization of hematite is ~200 times weaker than that of magnetite, the abundance of hematite in our samples should be much higher than that of magnetite. If the hematite was transformed from primary Ti ‐rich titanomagnetite by low‐temperature oxidation processes, then we would expect to see wildly distributed oxidation structures, yet we do not (Figures 6 and 7). These observations provide evidence that both magnetite and hematite were produced by high ‐temperature exsolution during initial cooling of the lava, an interpretation that is also supported by our magnetic petrography and geochemistry results (Figures 6 and 7). Conclusions New paleomagnetic directions were measured from 28 Middle Triassic volcanic sites around the Yanshiping town on the northern Qiangtang block. No obvious rock magnetic, petrographic, or paleomagnetic observa- tions indicate that the 28 site mean ChRMs directions are in ﬂuenced by unremoved or secondary magneti- zations. Furthermore, our data pass fold tests and appear to average secular variation. Our paleomagnetic data from Middle Triassic lavas locate the northern Qiangtang block at 23.0 ± 5.6°N at ~240 Ma at our refer- ence location (33.5°N, 92.0°E). The Yidun arc is a microblock in eastern Tibet located between the Hoh ‐Xil‐Songpan‐Ganzi (HXSG) basin to the north and the northern Qiangtang block to the south. The Yidun arc complex consists of Paleozoic limestones and ma ﬁc lavas and Triassic sediments, granitoids, and volcanic rocks (Wang et al., 2011). The HXSG basin is composed mostly of greenschist ‐facies turbidites and other deep ‐marine facies of Triassic age (Ding et al., 2013; Yin & Nie, 1993). Lower Triassic shallow marine limestone and interbedded conglomerates unconformably overlie Carboniferous ‐Permian strata along the northern and southern margins of the HXSG basin. The HXSG basin received ~2 × 10 6 km3 deep‐marine strata during the Middle to Late Triassic (Ding et al., 2013; Yin & Nie, 1993). Three end ‐member models have been proposed for the formation of the HXSG basin: (1) a remanent ocean basin (Zhou & Graham, 1996); (2) a rift basin (Chang, 2000); or (3) a Mediterranean ‐style back ‐arc basin (Ding et al., 2013; Klimetz, 1983; Pullen et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2014). Our study area lies south of Yanshiping town on the northern Qiangtang block. This location is between the Jinsha suture and Longmucuo ‐Shuanghu suture (Figure 1a). Mesozoic strata are abundant and out- crop well at our study area and are mainly composed of the Jurassic Yanshiping Group and Triassic Bagong and Bolila Formations. The Triassic Bolila Formation consists of limestones interbedded with silt- stones and shales. The conformably overlying Triassic Bagong Formation is predominantly composed of sandstones and siltstones. The Jurassic Yanshiping Group (comprising Quemoco, Buqu, Xiali, Suowa, and Xueshan Formations), overlies the Bagong Formation in angular unconformity. We report a well ‐dated paleomagnetic pole from the southern Lancangjiang volcanic belt in western Yunnan of China. Stable Characteristic Remanent Magnetizations (ChRMs) were isolated from 21 sites at high temperatures following step ‐wise thermal demagnetization. The data pass fold, reversal, and conglomerate tests and are interpreted to be primary thermal remanent magnetizations. The new paleomagnetic pole (46.1°N/176.2°E, K=44.9, A95=4.8°, N=21) yields a paleolatitude of 26.0 ± 4.8°N at the reference site (23.0°N/100.4°E) in the southern Lancangjiang area. This direct paleo ‐latitudinal constraint on the Paleo ‐Tethys suture zone in western Yunnan indicates that the north branch of the Paleo ‐Tethys Ocean closed no later than the Carnian Age of Late Triassic, and con ﬁrms a geographic linkage between the North Qiangtang and Indochina Blocks at least during the Early Permian to Late Triassic. A Abstract The tectonic evolution of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean, and in particular the time of its closure, is debated. A Abstract The tectonic evolution of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean, and in particular the time of its closure, is debated. Here we present new constraints on the evolution of this region from an integrated paleomagnetic and geochronologic study of the Late Triassic Batang Group volcanic rocks in Qamdo, Eastern Qiangtang Terrane (EQT). Two zircon U-Pb ages indicate that the volcanic rocks erupted at ∼227–222 Ma. New paleomagnetic results yield a robust Late Triassic paleopole of 57.6°N, 176.4°E (A95 = 7.8°), corresponding to a paleolatitude of 32.5 ± 7.8°N for the study area. Integrated with other lines of paleomagnetic and geological evidence, we show that the northward drift of the EQT placed it at the same paleolatitude as the Tarim Block by ∼227– 222 Ma, which suggests that the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean in the Qamdo region closed before that time, and likely around ∼230 Ma. Plain Language Summary The closure of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean, which was one of the most important ancient oceans of Asia, closed when the Qiangtang Terrane (QT) collided with the terranes now located to the north of it. The current model cannot explain the lack of mixing between boreal and Tethyan fauna in the XSB during the early Permian Abstract The paleogeographic position of the Xilinhot–Songliao Block (XSB) is crucial to understand the spatiotemporal relationship between the Paleo-Asian Ocean (PAO) and East Paleo-Tethys Ocean (EPTO) tectonic domains. However, the lack of robust early Permian paleomagnetic data in the XSB has led to uncertainty in its paleogeographic position. Here, we report a well-dated (286.1–281.25 Ma) paleomagnetic pole (38.4°N/17.6°E, A95 = 4.0°) from andesites of the Dashizhai Formation in the XSB. We combined our paleomagnetic data with available geological and paleontological data to reconstruct the paleogeographic relationship between the PAO and EPTO. The XSB was located on the northern margin of the EPTO at ∼285 Ma, suggesting that the northern boundary of the EPTO tectonic domain extended to the southern margin of the XSB, the Hegenshan Ocean (between the XSB and the Mongolia Block) corresponds to the eastern PAO, and the XSB separated the eastern PAO and EPTO at ∼285 Ma. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: ‐sen University, Guangzhou, China Abstract To better understand the rifting history and mechanism of the Indochina Block from eastern Gondwana, we report a paleomagnetic study on middle Carboniferous (~315 Ma) limestones from the southernmost Yunnan of China. Characteristic remanent magnetizations (ChRMs) were isolated from samples in 14 sites after secondary magnetizations were erased at relatively low temperature ranges, of which magnetites were interpreted to be the magnetic carriers for the former while goethites and pyrrhotites for the latter. The rock ‐magnetically interpreted minerals are con ﬁrmed with a scanning electron microscope (SEM) on samples with a high concentration of magnetic minerals, of which the calcium carbonates were dissolved with a mixed solution of CH 3COOH and CH 3COONa. The ChRMs passed reversal and fold tests and are very likely a primary magnetization, which correspond a paleomagnetic pole of 76.1°S/181.3°E ( A95 = 4.0°, N = 14) and locate the Indochina Block at 18.4 ± 4.0°S. A relatively quiet tectonic period was suggested for the North Qiangtang, Indochina, and South China blocks during the middle Carboniferous‐early Permian, and a sequential start of rapid drifting of these blocks was recognized, which is coeval with the rifting of Cimmerian terrane

Characteristic remanent magnetizations (ChRMs) were isolated from samples in 14 sites after secondary magnetizations were erased at relatively low temperature ranges, of which magnetites were interpreted to be the magnetic carriers for the former while goethites and pyrrhotites for the latter. (2003, 2009) correlated the closing of Paleo ‐Tethys Ocean and the accompanying opening of Neo ‐Tethys Ocean with the transformation of Pangea from an Early Permian Irvingian B con ﬁguration (Irving, 1977; Morel & Irving, 1981) to a Late Permian ‐Early Triassic Wegenerian A con ﬁguration (Bullard et al., 1965; Van der Voo, 1993). Six time intervals were sampled in the Donbas Foldbelt (eastern Ukraine), which was ﬁlled with sediments and volcanic units during the late Devonian to Permian syn- and post-rift subsidence phases. We present results from sediments that were corrected for inclination shallowing with the elongation/inclination ( E/I) method. Geological setting and petrography The Srednecheremshansk intrusion is located in the Irkut block of the Sharyzhalgay uplift within the Tungus superterrane of the southern part of the Siberian craton (Fig. 1a, b). The Sharyzhalgay uplift comprises two granite-greenstone (Onot and Bulun) and two granulite-gneiss (Irkut and Kitoy) blocks (Fig. 1b) (Grabkin and Melnikov, 1980). Blocks are mainly composed of Archean rocks and intruded by Paleo- proterozoic post-collisional granitoids (Fig. 1b) (Donskaya and Glad- kochub, 2021). Geological setting and petrography The Srednecheremshansk intrusion is located in the Irkut block of the Sharyzhalgay uplift within the Tungus superterrane of the southern part of the Siberian craton (Fig. 1a, b). The Sharyzhalgay uplift comprises two granite-greenstone (Onot and Bulun) and two granulite-gneiss (Irkut and Kitoy) blocks (Fig. 1b) (Grabkin and Melnikov, 1980). Blocks are mainly composed of Archean rocks and intruded by Paleo- proterozoic post-collisional granitoids (Fig. 1b) (Donskaya and Glad- kochub, 2021). The final assembly of all blocks probably took place in Paleoproterozoic, simultaneously with the formation of the Siberian craton (Donskaya, 2020). The Srednecheremshansk intrusion cuts Archean biotite and garnet- biotite gneisses of the Cheremshansk Fm. of the Irkut block of the Sharyzhalgay uplift (Fig. 1b, 2). A paleomagnetic study was carried out in the Ordovician granitoids located in the northeastern North Patagonian Gondwana Massif (NPM), close to Valcheta town (Río Negro Province, Argentina), to provide new evidence on the relation Paleomagnetism between Patagonia and Gondwana during the Early Paleozoic. A paleomagnetic paleopole (VA1) was calculated Patagonia out of 14 VGPs yielding a mean at 12.7◦N, 275.5◦E with K =13.3 and A95 =11.3◦. A second result (VA2-remag), Ordovician computed on other component found in 12 sites is located at 76.4◦S, 84◦E, K =11.8 and A95 =5◦. VA2-remag Valcheta fits very well with the Lower Jurassic segment of the apparent polar wander path of Gondwana. We interpret that it corresponds to a remagnetization carried mostly by high-coercitive components acquired during the hydro- thermal activity associated with the Early Jurassic effusion of the Marifil-Chon Aike volcanic province. VA1 paleopole becomes consistent with the Gondwana apparent polar wander path at ~450 Ma, after applying a 30–40◦CCW rotation of the NPM to restore a V-shaped basin (Sierra Grande sea) opened before Permian-Triassic times. This rotation restores the paleogeographical position of the Ordovician granites of northeast NPM to the south of the Sierras Pampeanas aligning them with the eastern domain of

onds to a remagnetization carried mostly by high-coercitive components acquired during the hydro- thermal activity associated with the Early Jurassic effusion of the Marifil-Chon Aike volcanic province. VA1 paleopole becomes consistent with the Gondwana apparent polar wander path at ~450 Ma, after applying a 30–40◦CCW rotation of the NPM to restore a V-shaped basin (Sierra Grande sea) opened before Permian-Triassic times. This rotation restores the paleogeographical position of the Ordovician granites of northeast NPM to the south of the Sierras Pampeanas aligning them with the eastern domain of the Famatinian orogenic and magmatic belt. VA1 paleopole suggests that the position of the NPM was close to the South American margin of Gondwana and separated by the Sierra Grande Sea from the Rio de la Plata-Kalahari cratons from, at least, late Ordovician times, which favors a para-autochthonous origin for the NPM. A former hypothesis suggesting a connection of the NPM and the TransAntarctic Mountains is unlikely for the late Ordovician according to our new data, which only allows an allochthonous NPM close to the Kalahari craton. 1. A paleomagnetic study was carried out in the Ordovician granitoids located in the northeastern North Patagonian Gondwana Massif (NPM), close to Valcheta town (Río Negro Province, Argentina), to provide new evidence on the relation Paleomagnetism between Patagonia and Gondwana during the Early Paleozoic. A paleomagnetic paleopole (VA1) was calculated Patagonia out of 14 VGPs yielding a mean at 12.7◦N, 275.5◦E with K =13.3 and A95 =11.3◦. A second result (VA2-remag), Ordovician computed on other component found in 12 sites is located at 76.4◦S, 84◦E, K =11.8 and A95 =5◦. omagnetism 20.2◦E, A95: 6.4◦, n: 30), that likely corresponds to a Permian remagnetization and suggests that such belt might extend further north than previously envisaged. We performed several rock-magnetic studies on this succession of laminated fine grain sandstones and siltstones in order to determine the magnetic phases that carry the remanence. Thermomagnetic (k vs. T) curves, field and frequency dependence of bulk susceptibility, hysteresis loops, isothermal remanent magnetization acquisition and back-field curves, three-axis IRM thermal demagne- tization, among others, permitted to establish magnetite as the main mineral carrying the remanence. Micro- scopic observations confirmed a secondary chemical origin for magnetite. Magnetic fabric studies indicate a tectonic fabric, consistent with cleavage developed on these rocks together with low-grade metamorphism. However, a Permian remagnetization, as suggested by the paleomagnetic pole position, cannot be related to Cambrian deformation and metamorphism and might be related to hydrothermal processes. 1.
